source.title: Investigating the Effect of Misalignment on Membership Privacy in the White-box Setting
source.authors: Ana-Maria Creţu; Daniel Jones; Yves-Alexandre de Montjoye; Shruti Tople

record.file_problem: none; full paper text, including appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study directly measures how similar internal model weights and activations are under different training conditions and after re-alignment. It uses weight distances and activation-based metrics rather than reproducing the original study's method.
record.gate_note: The paper measures alignment between target and shadow models, including several metrics and training-condition comparisons. MIA attack AUC results are not recorded as rows because they measure membership inference performance, not representational convergence. Values used to tune or select methods are also omitted.
record.test_reason: The study compares same-architecture CNN4 models trained from different seeds and data. It measures same-position weight distance (WMS), activation distance (AMS) and activation correlation (CBA), before and after permutation matching (including Li et al.'s correlation matching). This bears on V3/V4 (shared features up to permutation, mappability) and on V6/V7 (metric dependence, incompleteness). The method differs from Li et al.'s, so T2. MIA AUCs are attack performance, not convergence rates. However, Table 4 recovery of a meta-classifier's signal after re-alignment is indirect V4 evidence.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that a different weight initialisation is the main cause of shadow-model misalignment, which they read as similar features in permuted positions. Other randomness, disjoint data and a shifted distribution add little. Permutation re-alignment reduces misalignment but struggles with large and middle layers. Re-alignment strongly improves activation-based white-box MIAs, sometimes improves gradient-based ones, and never hurts.
record.recipe_differences: The study measures weight and activation alignment under controlled changes to training randomness and data, then tests permutation-based re-alignment. It does not reproduce the original convergence study's method.
record.method_sensitivity: Alignment depends strongly on whether weight initialisation differs, and varies by layer. The reported alignment procedures differ in effectiveness by layer; the third, large middle layer is especially difficult. The paper reports broadly similar trends across WMS, AMS, and CBA.

fits_no_version.finding: Same-position (unmatched) weight and activation alignment of same-architecture models is governed by shared initialisation. Changing batch order, dropout, overlap or disjoint data, or even the training distribution (CelebA ablations), adds little misalignment when initialisation is shared.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Shared initialisation, not shared data, determines whether same-architecture models' units align position-by-position.

record.problems: The study focuses mainly on same-task models and a small set of architectures; the CelebA distribution experiment is small, including only one shadow model for the same-distribution case. The paper notes that weight-distance and re-alignment measures are imperfect, and that middle layers are difficult to align. The selected comparisons use shared validation records and do not establish behaviour on broad out-of-distribution inputs.
record.rows_left_out: To stay within the 60-row cap, omitted Table 1 and Table 2 values for the second and fourth layers where not otherwise selected, along with Table 2 weight-sorting and re-alignment-after-initialisation results. Also omitted most Table 9–12 and Table 15 values and the remaining Table 13 conditions; these are reported as similar trends or additional metric/hyperparameter analyses in the appendices.

untested.parts: All: no scale or capability sweep, no cross-architecture or cross-objective comparison.
Subspace-level similarity (SVCCA/CKA), many-to-one unit matching, larger or deeper networks. Only CNN4 and MLP4 are matched, against one target per comparison.
General linear maps, stitching layers, relative representations, unpaired mapping, cross-architecture maps.
All: no interpretable features, SAE features or circuits.
Neighbour-based measures, measure hyperparameters, varied or OOD input sets.
Plateau with scale; shared objectives versus a common model of reality across different tasks.

missing.what: AMS and CBA after each re-alignment method (e.g. first-layer CBA 0.14→0.57, third 0.01→0.20). This is the main permutation-invariant evidence for V3/V4/V6/V7.
Random-permutation baselines for AMS and CBA (first-layer CBA 0.15, third 0.01), showing unaligned different-init values equal chance.
Re-alignment WMS for CNN4 on CIFAR100 and for MLP4 on Purchase100. On MLP4, correlation matching barely helps (e.g. 36.37→36.09 in the second layer).
CelebA same-randomness ablations (WMS 2.87 vs 2.96 first layer; 4.86 vs 4.51 third), on which the distribution claim rests.
Meta-classifier transfer after re-alignment: second-to-last layer OA AUC 0.509 unaligned vs 0.813 top-down matched vs 0.805 auditor.

record.verdict_notes: Not an original source, though it reuses Li et al.'s correlation matching. Most recorded rows are same-position measures, which cannot show V3-style sharing up to permutation. The convergence-relevant evidence is in the re-alignment rows and the unrecorded Table 15. Rows r19–r20 duplicate r17–r18.

versions.untested_parts: No scale sweep or comparison of model size and capability; no comparison across different architectures, objectives, or modalities as models become more capable.
No paired image-caption or other vision-language representations.

Same-task models are studied, chiefly CNN4 target/shadow models. The paper does not test broad feature inventories, shared subspaces across many architectures, or whether the same individual features recur across unrelated tasks.
Tests layer permutations and re-alignment techniques between same-architecture models. Does not test stitching, relative representations, unpaired mapping, or a general linear map's downstream loss.
No analysis of interpretable features, neurons, SAE features, or circuits recurring across models.

Compares weight distance, activation distance, and activation correlation, and includes a different-distribution experiment. Does not systematically vary similarity-measure settings, input datasets for all measures, or out-of-distribution inputs.

Studies training randomness and data choices for same-task models. Does not compare different objectives or establish a general explanation based on shared objectives versus a common model of reality.

relationships.condition: Different-init CNN4 models, first (lower) layers, after permutation matching
relationships.reason: First-layer WMS falls from 12.44 to 8.87–10.80 (r22, r25, r28, r31). Per Table 15 (text), CBA rises from 0.14 to 0.56–0.57, and Fig. 1d shows matched features.
relationships.display_finding: Matching reduced first-layer WMS from 12.44 to 8.87–10.80 and increased CBA from 0.14 to 0.56–0.57.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.condition: Different-init CNN4 models, first (lower) layers, after permutation matching
source_check.reason: First-layer weight distances decrease and matched activation maps demonstrate shared features across initializations. Correct the supporting CBA range: Table 15B gives 0.52, 0.45, 0.56 and 0.57 for bottom-up weight, top-down weight, activation and correlation matching, respectively; 0.56–0.57 describes only the latter two.

relationships.condition: Large middle (third, 500-unit) layer of different-init models
relationships.reason: Matching barely lowers WMS (r23, r26, r29, r32). Per Table 15 (text), CBA reaches only 0.12–0.20, so far fewer shared features are recoverable in upper layers.
relationships.display_finding: Matching barely reduced WMS in the third, 500-unit layer, while CBA reached only 0.12–0.20.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.condition: Large middle (third, 500-unit) layer of different-init models
source_check.reason: Weight-distance reductions are small and recovered same-position activation correlations remain low. Correct the range to 0.08–0.20 across the four matching methods; CBA does not quantify the fraction of shared features or exclude shared subspaces.

relationships.reason: WMS drops from 12.87 to 5.71, below the same-init adversary's 7.55 (r27). Table 4 (text) shows re-aligned shadow activations restore MIA AUC from 0.509 to 0.813.
relationships.display_finding: WMS decreased from 12.87 to 5.71, below the same-initialization adversary's 7.55, while realignment raised membership inference AUC from 0.509 to 0.813.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.reason: Table 2 gives fourth-layer WMS 12.87→5.71, below the same-initialization condition's 7.55. Table 4 gives activation-based MIA AUC 0.509→0.813 after top-down matching, supporting task-specific transfer. Those activation features are outputs of the third, second-to-last layer, not fourth-layer outputs.

relationships.condition: Permutation maps for first to third layers
relationships.reason: Residual distances stay well above same-init levels, and the third layer barely changes (r22–r26, r28–r33). The map is restricted to permutations.
relationships.display_finding: Residual distances remained well above same-initialization levels, and third-layer alignment barely changed them.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.condition: Permutation maps for first to third layers
source_check.reason: Table 2 shows substantial residual distances, particularly in the third layer, and Section 5 describes imperfect matching and propagated errors. This qualifies the tested permutation maps; it does not establish failure of more general linear maps.

relationships.condition: Re-aligned third layer: weight-based vs activation-based metrics
relationships.reason: WMS improves only about 5% (r23), while CBA rises from 0.01 to 0.20 and AMS falls from 27.90 to 24.07 (Table 15, text). The authors call the layer more aligned despite WMS.
relationships.display_finding: Realignment improved WMS by only about 5%, while CBA rose from 0.01 to 0.20 and AMS fell from 27.90 to 24.07.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.condition: Re-aligned third layer: weight-based vs activation-based metrics
source_check.reason: Section 5 explicitly contrasts a small WMS improvement with significant activation-metric improvements. The stated numerical example mixes methods: bottom-up weight matching gives WMS 30.98→29.35, CBA 0.01→0.12 and AMS 27.90→25.79; activation matching gives CBA 0.20 and AMS 24.07.
